content: Falls can occur in any workplace, regardless of the industry or setting. However, fall-related injuries are entirely preventable with proper measures in place. Falls are one of the most common workplace injuries. The construction industry experiences the highest number of fatalities due to falls, with most of these incidents involving falls from heights. In contrast, nonfatal fall injuries are most frequently reported in the educational, health services, healthcare, and social assistance sectors. These injuries typically involve slips and falls occurring on the same level. Other industries with a high risk of fall-related injuries include nursing and residential care facilities, ambulance services, building cleaning and maintenance, and transportation and material moving. In 2020, 805 workers lost their lives due to falls, and 211,640 workers in the private sector sustained serious injuries that required time away from work. The financial impact of fall-related injuries is significant. In the United States alone, the combined costs of workers' compensation and medical expenses for workplace falls are estimated to reach $70 billion annually. This issue is not confined to the U.S.; other countries also face similar challenges, prompting the global public health community to prioritize strategies for reducing fall injuries. Falls are the leading cause of fatalities among construction workers. To address this, a national campaign has been launched to prevent fatal falls. As part of this initiative, an annual National Stand-Down event is held to emphasize fall prevention. Common safety risks associated with workplace falls include unprotected edges, improperly positioned ladders, misuse of fall protection equipment, slippery surfaces caused by water, grease, or other contaminants, clutter and tripping hazards in walkways, and irregularities in flooring or wall openings. Federal regulations and industry standards outline specific measures and recommendations for fall prevention and protection. Despite these guidelines, unsafe practices and a lack of strong safety culture in many industries contribute to consistently high rates of fall injuries each year. To reduce these rates, it is essential to: Implement innovative and effective fall prevention and protection technologies. Use appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), such as harnesses, fall guards, and slip-resistant footwear. Foster a culture of safety by educating the workforce on best practices. Achieving these goals requires collaboration among various stakeholders, including regulators, industry leaders, professional associations, labor unions, employers, employees, safety professionals, and researchers. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) Division of Safety Research (DSR) conducts extensive research to prevent work-related injuries and fatalities caused by falls across all industries. Their Traumatic Occupational Injury Research Labs focus on developing and evaluating strategies to mitigate these risks. As a leader in occupational safety research, NIOSH plays a critical role in fall-injury prevention efforts. Their strategic planning and goal-setting processes are informed by factors such as the scale and urgency of the problem, available resources and expertise, current research, the strength of partnerships, and the progress of research-to-practice initiatives. Input from the National Academy of Sciences program review further enhances these efforts. NIOSH also provides resources to support fall prevention, including infographics, posters, and access to the NIOSHTIC-2 database, which contains occupational safety and health publications funded by NIOSH. For example, one infographic highlights how slip-resistant shoes can reduce slip injuries among food service workers.
